title: Hurricane Isaias forecast to strengthen to category three before landfall in US
summary: El Niño has led to a quiet season so far but the first Atlantic hurricane of the year is set to make landfall later on Friday into Saturday across the US Gulf Coast.
text: Hurricane Isaias: Expected to strengthen to category three before making landfall - BBC Weather BBC Homepage Skip to content Accessibility Help Your account Home News Sport Earth Reel Worklife Travel Culture Future Music TV Weather Sounds More menu More menu Search BBC Home News Sport Earth Reel Worklife Travel Culture Future Music TV Weather Sounds Close menu BBC Weather Menu Home Weather Warnings Flood Warnings Monthly Outlook Coast and Sea Help Hurricane Isaias forecast to strengthen to category three before landfall in US Image source, Zoom Earth Image caption, Hurricane Isaias is starting to develop an eye as it strengthens in the Gulf of Mexico as a category two storm By Ben Rich and Simon King , Lead Weather Presenters Published 7 October 2026 Updated 4 hours ago Isaias, the first hurricane of the Atlantic season has been continuing to strengthen and is now expected to become a major storm. Early on Friday morning it became a category two hurricane with sustained wind speeds of 104mph (170km/h) but will briefly develop further into a category three - a major hurricane - in the coming hours. It has the potential to bring damaging winds, torrential rain and a storm surge to parts of the US Gulf Coast with landfall expected late Friday. Hurricane and Storm Surge Watches have been issued. Isaias brings an end to the lack of hurricanes that has led to a record-breakingly quiet Atlantic season so far with development suppressed by the growing El Niño pattern . Developing El Niño becomes strongest on record weeks before expected peak Published 22 September Hurricanes: Inside the deadly storms What track will Hurricane Isaias take? In its latest update, the US National Hurricane Center estimates that hurricane Isaias will intensify further with wind speeds of up to 115mph (185km/h) - category three - by Friday afternoon local US time. Isaias is then expected to weaken slightly before making landfall on the Gulf Coast, across Alabama and the Florida Panhandle late Friday night and in the early hours of Saturday local time. After landfall it will head north through Alabama, brushing the east of Missouri during Saturday. While it will quickly weaken to a tropical storm, it will still bring some dangerous winds and flooding rains. Image caption, Damaging winds, torrential rain and coastal flooding are the major risks from the developing hurricane A dangerous storm sturge of up to 6ft is expected in Alabama and Florida, especially around high tide and it will be accompanied by strong winds and large waves. Between 4 and 8in (101-203mm) of rain is expected in southern Alabama, the Florida panhandle and Big Bend, and southwest Georgia. A few places could see up to 15in (381mm) with possible flash flooding, especially in urban areas, and the risk of isolated river flooding. The US National Weather Service has issued Hurricane and Storm Surge Watches along the Gulf Coast. Florida Governor Ron DeSantis has declared a state of emergency across 25 counties over concerns about potential impacts. Several major sporting events throughout the region have been cancelled or rescheduled due to the incoming storm. The highly-anticipated football match between the University of Georgia and the University of Alabama - due to be attended by President Donald Trump in the city of Tuscaloosa - is still expected to take place on Saturday. As the storm moves further inland and loses contact with its warm water fuel source it will weaken. But it is still expected to bring some potentially disruptive wet weather for large swathes of the south-east USA as far north as the Tennessee Valley and the Carolinas. El Niño brings an eerily quiet hurricane season so far Forecasters in the US had predicted the 2026 hurricane season would be quieter than average citing the developing strong El Niño in the Pacific Ocean. An El Niño weather event can lead to more wind shear over the Caribbean and Atlantic, which tears storms apart before they have time to develop. Whilst lowering the odds of hurricane formation, it does not make it impossible. Isaias has managed to form in an area with limited wind shear and very high sea temperatures - currently 30 or 31C - giving it the fuel it needs to grow. Forecasters expect it to encounter more wind shear as it moves northwards over the next few days which should limit its intensification somewhat - but exact forecasts are likely to shift over the coming days.
